sentences.text: The Council Fire.
first voice.
My grandmother told me a person should always say who they are before they tell a story, so the ancestors know who is speaking.
So.
My name is a braid of twelve names from twelve corners of the world, and I will tell you them at the end, when you have earned them.
I am seven generations down from the people in this book.

I am holding, as I write this, a lump of coal, an amber bead, a carved stone llama, a smooth river stone worn by many thumbs, a black go stone, a stone cross, a mala of bodhi seeds, a pounamu, a lump of spinifex resin, a beaded bracelet, a granite clan stone, and a rice seed—the tokens they carried, that came down to me.
I live in a world they made out of the broken one.
It is hard here, and it is good.
They left this record so we would know it had been done before.
So that if it ever broke again, we would not be afraid, because we would have the map.
They wrote it as a warning, for their own time, and as a map, for mine.
Both came true.
I will let you decide which mattered more.
That is what the twelve broke.
Not the heat.
The silence.
They found each other, and they made the words, and once there were words there could be a council.
The Council Fire.
Part Three — What They Built.
The great towers still marched across the desert, the wires that had carried coal-fired electricity off to light distant cities while families beneath them lived without power.
The wires were empty now.
And the desert sat in the dead center of the sun’s country.
“They offered us a royalty,” Nizhoní told the council, and her voice went cold and clear the way it did.
“The same shape as the coal deal.
Let an outside company own the sun off our land, take the wealth down the wire, leave us a check and a hole.
I told them no.
I told them: the sun is not a thing under the ground that runs out.
It comes back every morning, free, forever, on our land.
We will not rent it.
We will own it.”
The others nodded.
Vahan spoke of the wheel of eternity his people had carved into stone for a thousand years.
Lobsang spoke of the sun that had always been sacred to the Tibetan Buddhists.
Te Rangi spoke of the waves.
Warrun spoke of the sun.
Kiprono spoke of the water.
Hamish spoke of the wind.
Chariya spoke of the rice.
They all agreed: the energy was theirs, and they would own it.
So they built the thing the dying world could not imagine: power generated on the people’s land, owned by the people, the wealth circling home.
Corn under the solar panels, food and power off the same acre.
